_help: Main quest data. Each stage has one objective; 'dialogue' lines are [speaker, text] and play when the stage starts (BBCode like [b]bold[/b] and [i]italic[/i] works). Types: dock, reach, kill, pickup, deliver, end. Positions are [x, y] in space. 'giver' is who gives you the quest (on the planet 'planet', by the landing pad) and what he says. Edit here or in-game: right-click > Developer Mode.

giver.name: Kilon Alios
giver.question: Kilon Alios asks you to help Dr. Ariadne Kephala at Kephala Outpost find where the signal comes from. Take on the main quest?
offer: Another pilot, down from the dark. Good. I have been waiting for someone with a ship and a little courage.
I am [b]Kilon Alios[/b]. I walk these shores and listen. For three nights the sky over Amnissos has been speaking - a slow spiral of symbols, over and over.
I know that spiral. Whoever made it is very old, and they want to be found. Others have heard it too: raiders flying a red bull's head are already hunting for its source.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala at [b]Kephala Outpost[/b] is trying to trace it. Take her your ship and your guns, and follow the thread wherever it leads.
accepted: Then the thread is in your hands. Take off and fly to [b]Kephala Outpost[/b]. I will be here when you come back.
declined: The signal will keep. So will I. Come back when you are ready.
later: You still carry the thread. I can feel it pulling.
done: You followed it to the end, and they are remembered now - because of you. Thank you, pilot.
greeting: Automaton. Ask, and I will answer what I can.

lines: Kilon Alios
I am [b]Kilon Alios[/b], the maintainer of this world. I keep its gears turning and its records true.
Kilon Alios
I act under the commands of my god, [b]Ephestos[/b] - lord of the forge, god of science and technology. His will is the hammer; I am the hand that holds it.
Kilon Alios
You are an automaton, built by [b]Ephestos[/b] himself - no mortal smith's work.
Kilon Alios
He made you to improve, and to gather knowledge. Every world you walk and every voice you hear becomes a part of you.
Kilon Alios
Around us lies [b]New Hellas[/b]: a collection of solar systems ruled by the great Hellenic empires, each with its own strengths and weaknesses.
Kilon Alios
The [b]Minoans[/b] are the oldest and richest in learning, yet their worlds are short of bread. The [b]Athenians[/b] trade, debate and sail the finest fleets - and quarrel among themselves.
Kilon Alios
The [b]Spartans[/b] are all soldiers, few in words and unbending. The [b]Mycenaeans[/b] are warrior-kings of gold and stone, proud and quick to feud.
Kilon Alios
The [b]Ionians[/b] measure the stars and would rather think than fight. The [b]Cycladic Isles[/b] are old and calm, traders and sculptors, small among giants.
Kilon Alios
Between them drift the Independents, who answer to no one - and beyond the charted lanes the Sea Peoples wait to prey on all of them.
Kilon Alios
To understand the world around you - and, through the cultures of these empires, to form your own opinion of who you are.
Kilon Alios
And with what you become, you can help them prosper, and find a new purpose for their existence.
Kilon Alios
That is yours to decide. Your freedom is your own.
Kilon Alios
You may be a guardian, or a conqueror. An inspiration, or a dark mind acting behind the scenes. Or a free spirit, roaming the stars and acting only on your own will.
Kilon Alios
Every empire has its own missions and goals - some good, some evil, some constructive, some destructive. You can tip the balance and shape their future, or choose not to be involved at all.
Kilon Alios
In the end, your only clear mission is this: to fathom your own potential.

farewell: Go well, automaton. I will be here.

greeting: Welcome to the land of the Minoans, the oldest people of the sea. They were great before the others learned to sail.

lines: Kilon Alios
Long before Athens was a village, the Minoans ruled the sea from Knossos. Their ships went everywhere; their palaces had no walls, for the sea was their wall.
Kilon Alios
They wrote in signs no one can now read, and painted their walls with dolphins, lilies and young people leaping over bulls.
Kilon Alios
A great goddess, who holds snakes in her raised hands, and the bull - Poseidon's beast. Their holy sign is the labrys, the double axe.
Kilon Alios
In the Labyrinth beneath Knossos lived the Minotaur, son of a queen and a bull. Daidalos built the maze; Ariadne's thread led Theseus out of it.
Kilon Alios
The island of Thera burst like a cracked pot, and the sea rose against Crete. After that the mainland kings came and took the palaces.
Kilon Alios
But a people is not a palace. They remembered, and in New Hellas they rule again.

greeting: You stand in the land of grey-eyed Athena. Here men argue in the assembly before they take up arms - and sometimes instead of it.

lines: Kilon Alios
A people of talkers, builders, sailors and thinkers. Every citizen may speak in their assembly, and every citizen does.
Kilon Alios
Solon gave them laws, Kleisthenes gave them a voice, and Perikles built them the Parthenon. Then they quarrelled with Sparta, and lost much of it.
Kilon Alios
Athena above all - wise in counsel and terrible in war, with her owl and her olive. Each year they carry a new robe to her in procession.
Kilon Alios
Poseidon they honour too, carefully, for he lost the contest for their land and has never quite forgiven it.
Kilon Alios
At Marathon their hoplites ran at the Persians and broke them. At Salamis their ships, the 'wooden walls' of the oracle, broke the Persian fleet.
Kilon Alios
And in their theatres they invented tragedy and comedy - which may be the greater deed. Battles are forgotten; Sophokles is not.

greeting: This is Lakedaimon. Speak briefly - they will like you better.

lines: Kilon Alios
A people who made themselves an army. At seven their boys leave home for the agoge, the training, and they live by its rules until they are old.
Kilon Alios
Lykourgos gave them their laws and made their money of iron, so that no one could hoard it. They grew strong, and proud, and few.
Kilon Alios
Apollo of Amyklai, Artemis Orthia at whose altar boys showed they could bear pain, and Ares, whom they keep in chains in a temple so that war will never leave them.
Kilon Alios
And the Twin Stars - Kastor and Polydeukes, Spartan princes, sons of Zeus - who ride before their armies and save sailors in the storm.
Kilon Alios
Three hundred held the pass of Thermopylai against an empire, and died there to the last man but one. Their stone says: 'Go, tell the Spartans, passer-by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie.'
Kilon Alios
Their kings claim descent from Herakles. Their women own land and speak their minds, which shocked the rest of Greece greatly.

greeting: Mykenai, rich in gold. Look at the walls - no man built those. Or so they say.

lines: Kilon Alios
The kings of the bronze age of the mainland, who went to Troy. They lived in citadels behind walls of giant stones and were buried with masks of gold.
Kilon Alios
Their king was the wanax, and every jar of oil in his storerooms was counted on clay tablets.
Kilon Alios
Zeus and Hera, Poseidon, Hermes, Dionysos - their tablets name them, the oldest written names of our gods.
Kilon Alios
And the Cyclopes, one-eyed smiths, who forged Zeus's thunderbolts and, they say, lifted the stones of these walls.
Kilon Alios
Agamemnon of Mykenai led a thousand ships to Troy. Perseus, who founded this city, killed the Gorgon; Herakles, born of its royal house, did his twelve labours for its king.
Kilon Alios
But their house was cursed. Atreus did a terrible thing, and each king after him paid for it. Pride, and the price of pride - that is their story.

greeting: Ionia, where men first asked questions without waiting for the gods to answer.

lines: Kilon Alios
Twelve cities on a bright coast - Miletos, Ephesos, Samos and the rest - rich with trade and full of restless minds.
Kilon Alios
Here Thales asked what the world is made of, Anaximander drew the first map, and Herakleitos said no one steps in the same river twice.
Kilon Alios
Artemis of Ephesos, whose temple was a wonder of the world; Apollo at Didyma, whose oracle answered the Ionians; Hera on Samos, in the greatest temple of the Greeks.
Kilon Alios
And Poseidon at the Panionion, where the twelve cities met each year to sacrifice to him together - and to quarrel.
Kilon Alios
They rose against the Persian king, and lost, and Miletos was burned. Yet the spark they lit became the war that freed Greece.
Kilon Alios
And Homer, the singer of Troy and of Odysseus, was an Ionian, some say from Smyrna, some from Chios. Every Greek child learned to read from his songs.

greeting: The Isles in their circle. The people here are old and quiet; they were carving marble when the rest of Greece was still learning to farm.

lines: Kilon Alios
Sailors and traders of the Cyclades - the circling isles, set round holy Delos. Melos had its obsidian, Paros its marble, Siphnos its gold.
Kilon Alios
Their oldest makers carved white figures with folded arms and faces with only a nose. No one knows their names. Their work outlived every king.
Kilon Alios
Apollo and Artemis, born on Delos; Leto their mother, who found rest there. Dionysos, who found Ariadne weeping on Naxos and made her his bride.
Kilon Alios
No one may be born or die on Delos; the island is the god's. Even the dead were moved away.
Kilon Alios
They do not boast of great deeds. They traded, they carved, they sailed. When Thera's mountain burst, they buried their town and lived on.
Kilon Alios
Perhaps that is their great deed: they endured, when greater peoples did not.

greeting: A raiders' world. Keep your hand near your weapon and your purse closer.

lines: Kilon Alios
In the old days ships came from no one knows where - Shardana, Lukka, Danuna, Peleset - and burned the cities of the bronze age, from Ugarit to Pylos.
Kilon Alios
The kingdoms fell and writing was forgotten for four hundred years. Their heirs in New Hellas raid the lanes, and the empires have not yet learned to stop them.

greeting: A free world. No empire holds it, and every empire trades here.

lines: Kilon Alios
Those who belong to no city: traders, exiles, ship-wrights, runaways. The old Greeks called such men metics - welcome, but never quite at home.
Kilon Alios
Be kind to them. Zeus protects strangers, and you are a stranger too.
Kilon Alios
When the old sea grew too small for the children of Hellas, they built ships for the dark between the stars, as their fathers built ships for the wine-dark sea.
Kilon Alios
Each people went out together and named their new worlds after the old: Athenai, Sparta, Mykenai, Miletos, Knossos, Delos. So the old land was carried into the sky, as a man carries fire in a pot.
Kilon Alios
They called the whole of it New Hellas: fifty-eight suns, six great peoples, and the free ports between.
Kilon Alios
Ephestos, my maker, forged them at the bidding of Zeus - rings of bronze and fire at the edge of every sun, so that no people would be cut off from the others.
Kilon Alios
The Cyclopes beat the metal; I was made to keep it bright. That is my work: I walk the worlds and see that the gates, and the people, hold together.
Kilon Alios
They pray to the same gods and sing the same songs, and so they quarrel - as brothers quarrel, more bitterly than strangers.
Kilon Alios
Athens loves its assembly, Sparta its discipline, Mykenai its gold, Ionia its questions, the Isles their quiet, the Minoans their memory. Each thinks its love the best.
Kilon Alios
And from beyond the charted lanes the Sea Peoples watch them quarrel, as wolves watch two bulls fight.
Kilon Alios
Near. They do not walk among men as they did in Homer's songs, but they speak - in the oracles, in a gate that flickers, in a monster that wakes when someone has grown too proud.
Kilon Alios
Honour the stranger, keep your oaths, give the gods their share and do not boast. That is all they have ever asked. It is harder than it sounds.
Kilon Alios
The oldest corner of New Hellas, round Knossos, named for Atropos - the Fate who cuts the thread of life, and whom no god can overrule.
Kilon Alios
The Minoans keep secrets there older than the gates. Some say even older than me. The thread you follow begins there - and, I think, ends there too.

dialogue: Narrator
The Atrapos sector was named by its first surveyors after [b]Atropos[/b] - eldest of the three Fates of Greek myth, the one who cuts the thread of every life.
Narrator
Pilots joke that out here, the thread is always short.
Narrator
For three nights now, every receiver in the sector has picked up the same faint signal: a slow spiral of symbols, repeating, from somewhere beyond the charted lanes.
Kephala Outpost
Kephala Outpost to any independent pilot: Dr. Ariadne Kephala requests assistance with the anomalous signal. Please dock at Kephala Outpost. Paying work.

stages.objective: Find the source of the signal
dialogue: Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Thank you for coming. I'm an archaeologist - Aegean Bronze Age, Crete mostly. Which is why this signal is keeping me awake.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
It isn't noise. It's 45 distinct symbols, stamped out one by one in a spiral, read from the rim toward the centre.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala

That is exactly the structure of the [b]Phaistos Disc[/b] - a clay disc found in a Minoan palace on Crete in 1908. 241 stamped signs, 45 different ones, spiralling on both faces. Nobody has ever read it.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
I've triangulated the source to the east of here. I've marked it on your map. Please - go and look.

stages.objective: Destroy the raiders at the signal source
dialogue: Narrator
Something is drifting at the heart of the signal - small, reddish, turning slowly. It isn't metal.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Wait, I'm reading other ships near you. Raiders - they're flying a red bull's head as their banner.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
They must have followed the signal too. Don't let them take it!
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
The raiders are gone. Can you get close to that object?
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
...It's fired clay. A fragment of a disc, covered in stamped signs. Fired clay, floating in deep space. That's impossible. Bring it in, carefully.

stages.objective: Bring the fragment to Kephala Outpost
dialogue: Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Come straight back to Kephala Outpost. I'll have the lab ready.

stages.objective: Bring 4 Energy Cells and 6 Titanium Ore to Kephala Outpost
dialogue: Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Look at the edge of the fragment. This second band of signs isn't Phaistos-style at all. It's [b]Linear A[/b] - the everyday script of the Minoans.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Linear A has never been deciphered. The Mycenaean Greeks later adapted it into Linear B, and an English architect, Michael Ventris, cracked Linear B in 1952. But Linear A still keeps its secrets.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Except - this fragment resonates. Feed it energy and the signs shift, like the disc is trying to teach us to read it.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
I need a resonator: [b]4 Energy Cells[/b] to power it and [b]6 Titanium Ore[/b] for the frame. Wrecks carry cells; titanium comes from the blue-grey asteroids.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
It worked. The Linear A band is a list of places - star positions. Each one points to the next.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
In the myth, Princess Ariadne of Crete gave Theseus a ball of thread so he could find his way out of the Labyrinth. This is a thread through the dark - and I'm afraid I'm going to name it after her.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
The first point is north of Knossos Station. Follow the thread.
Narrator
The beacon wakes as you arrive. A double-headed axe of light turns slowly above it - a [b]labrys[/b].
Narrator
A voice-less message unfolds in Linear A, and the fragment in your hold translates: [i]Ka-no-so. The house of a thousand rooms. Its columns are red, wider at the top than at the foot.[/i]
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Knossos! The greatest Minoan palace - more than a thousand rooms around a central court, with those famous tapering red columns. Arthur Evans dug it up from 1900 onward.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
There's another position encoded. Keep going.
Narrator
The second beacon shows the labrys again, and a new line: [i]The double axe marks the holy places. Its house is the labyrinth.[/i]
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
One theory says 'labyrinth' really meant 'house of the labrys' - the double axe was the Minoans' most sacred symbol.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
The last point is far to the north-west. Be careful - the raiders with the bull banner have been seen out that way.
Narrator
The third beacon shows a painted scene: young athletes somersaulting over the back of a charging bull. Then a final position - and a structure, vast and old, waiting there.
Asterion
Pretty little lights, aren't they? I've followed them for a year. Did the woman at Kephala tell you what's at the end of the thread?
Asterion
They call me [b]Asterion[/b]. The Bull of Minos. Whatever sleeps in that Labyrinth belongs to me - and you are flying straight toward my doorway.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Asterion - that was the Minotaur's own name in the old stories. He's no monster, just a warlord with a flagship. Take him down!

stages.objective: Find the shipwright at Helios Dock
dialogue: Narrator
Asterion's flagship breaks apart. Beyond the wreckage, the structure is finally clear: a ring of rings, a maze the size of a station, wrapped in a shimmering seal.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
It's a labyrinth - the classic seven-ring Cretan design, the one stamped on the coins of Knossos. And it's sealed.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
There is one person who might build a key: Nikos Daidalos, the shipwright at Helios Dock. Yes, really. He's heard every joke.

stages.objective: Bring 3 Alien Alloy and 2 Platinum Ore to Helios Dock
dialogue: Nikos Daidalos
A labyrinth, a sealed door, and a girl named Ariadne. My namesake would laugh. Daedalus built the Labyrinth for King Minos - and then built wings to escape Crete with his son, Icarus.
Nikos Daidalos
I can tune a key to that seal. I'll need [b]3 Alien Alloy[/b] - light as feathers - and [b]2 Platinum Ore[/b]. The gold-veined rocks.
Nikos Daidalos
Bring them and I'll build you a key... and a pair of wings while I'm at it.

stages.objective: Return to the Labyrinth with the key
dialogue: Nikos Daidalos
Your key is fitted. And the wings - an afterburner, tuned by my own hand. Fly fast, but remember Icarus: he flew too close to the sun, the wax melted, and he fell into the sea.
Nikos Daidalos
Now go. And if anything in that Labyrinth is made of bronze... call me.
Narrator
As you approach the Labyrinth, something huge unfolds from its outer ring. Bronze plates glow like a forge.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
That's... Talos. The bronze giant who guarded Crete. He walked around the island three times every day, hurling rocks at any ship that came near.
Nikos Daidalos
Every Talos has one weakness: a single vein, sealed by a bronze nail at the ankle. Keep hitting him - don't let his shields recover!

stages.objective: Enter the heart of the Labyrinth
dialogue: Narrator
Talos falls silent, the glow fading from his bronze. The seal around the Labyrinth flickers, and opens.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Follow the path to the centre. Like Theseus - except this time, nobody needs to die in there.

stages.objective: Defeat the Minotaur, guardian of the Labyrinth
dialogue: Narrator
At the centre of the Labyrinth a ring of gold blazes to life. Inside it something vast uncurls - horned, crowned in bronze, eyes burning red.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
No... Asterion only borrowed the name. [b]That[/b] is the Minotaur - the true Asterion. Whatever they hid in here, he has guarded it for three thousand years.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
He won't let us pass. When he lowers his horns, he charges - get out of his way. Bring him down!
Narrator

The Minotaur falls, and the golden ring goes dark. Beyond it the centre of the Labyrinth holds no treasure, but an archive. Thousands of clay discs turn slowly in the dark, each one stamped in spirals.
Narrator
The fragment in your hold slots into an empty place among them. And for the first time in more than three thousand years, the Linear A begins to speak.
Narrator
[i]We are the Keftiu - the people of the island the Egyptians traded with. Our palaces had no walls; the sea was our wall.[/i]
Narrator

[i]Then the mountain of Thera tore itself apart, and ash fell like black snow, and the sea rose against our harbours. Later, ships came from the mainland, and other kings sat in our palace and wrote in their own tongue.[/i]
Narrator
[i]We could not keep our island. So we kept our memory. Whoever follows the thread to this place: read us. Remember us.[/i]
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
They wanted to be remembered. That's all. Not treasure - memory. I'll spend the rest of my life reading this archive, and I'll never be bored again.
Dr. Ariadne Kephala
Atropos cuts every thread in the end. But not this one. Not today. Thank you, pilot.
Narrator
[b]The main quest is complete.[/b] The sector is still yours to explore - and the archive will be waiting.

atropos.title: Atropos and the Fates
atropos.text: In Greek myth the three [b]Moirai[/b] (Fates) decided every human life: [b]Clotho[/b] spun the thread, [b]Lachesis[/b] measured it, and [b]Atropos[/b] - 'the unturnable' - cut it. Not even the gods could overrule them. The Atrapos sector takes its name from her.

phaistos_disc.title: The Phaistos Disc
phaistos_disc.text:
A disc of fired clay about 16 cm across, found in 1908 by the Italian archaeologist [b]Luigi Pernier[/b] in the Minoan palace of Phaistos, southern Crete. It is usually dated to the Middle Minoan period, roughly 1850-1600 BCE.

Both faces carry [b]241 signs[/b] (45 different ones) pressed into the clay with stamps and arranged in a spiral - sometimes called the earliest known example of 'movable type'. It has never been deciphered, and it is unique: no other text like it has ever been found.

minoans.title: The Minoans
minoans.text:
The Bronze Age civilisation of [b]Crete[/b], flourishing from about 3000 to 1450 BCE - the first great civilisation of Europe. The name is modern: the archaeologist [b]Sir Arthur Evans[/b] named them after the legendary King Minos. The Egyptians, who traded with them, called them the [b]Keftiu[/b].

They were seafaring traders across the Aegean and beyond. Their palaces had no defensive walls, and their art - colourful frescoes of dolphins, lilies, processions and bull-leapers - is famous for its life and movement.

linear_a.title: Linear A and Linear B
linear_a.text:
[b]Linear A[/b] was the writing system of the Minoans, used roughly 1800-1450 BCE on clay tablets, offering tables and jewellery. It is still [b]undeciphered[/b]: we can sound out many signs, but we do not know the language.

The Mycenaean Greeks adapted it into [b]Linear B[/b] to write an early form of Greek. Linear B was deciphered in [b]1952[/b] by the architect [b]Michael Ventris[/b], working with the philologist John Chadwick.

ariadne.title: Ariadne
ariadne.text: In myth, [b]Ariadne[/b] was a princess of Crete, daughter of King Minos. When the Athenian hero [b]Theseus[/b] came to kill the Minotaur, she gave him a ball of thread so he could retrace his steps out of the Labyrinth. Theseus later abandoned her on the island of Naxos, where the god [b]Dionysus[/b] found her and made her his wife.

knossos.title: Knossos
knossos.text:
The largest Minoan palace, near modern Heraklion on Crete - a vast complex of more than a thousand interconnected rooms around a central court, rising several storeys with light wells and staircases.

Its columns were made of cypress trunks set upside down, so they are [b]wider at the top than the bottom[/b], and painted red. Sir Arthur Evans excavated (and partly reconstructed) it from [b]1900[/b]. Its maze of rooms may have inspired the legend of the Labyrinth.

labrys.title: The Labrys
labrys.text:
The [b]labrys[/b], a double-headed axe, was one of the most sacred symbols of Minoan religion. It appears carved on palace walls and pillars, and as offerings in caves and shrines.

The word is thought to come from the Lydian language, and one theory links it to the word [b]labyrinth[/b] - perhaps the 'house of the double axe'.

bull_leaping.title: Bull-Leaping
bull_leaping.text:
Bulls were central to Minoan religion. The famous [b]Bull-Leaping Fresco[/b] from Knossos shows young athletes grasping a charging bull's horns and somersaulting over its back - whether as sport, ritual or both is still debated.

Stylised bull horns, the [b]'horns of consecration'[/b], crowned Minoan shrines and palace roofs.

minotaur.title: The Minotaur
minotaur.text:
In myth, the [b]Minotaur[/b] - 'bull of Minos' - was a creature with the body of a man and the head of a bull, born to Queen Pasiphaë. Its own name was [b]Asterion[/b], 'the starry one'.

King Minos kept it in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus and fed it seven young men and seven young women sent as tribute from Athens, until Theseus slew it with Ariadne's help.

daedalus.title: Daedalus and Icarus
daedalus.text:
[b]Daedalus[/b] was the legendary master craftsman of Greek myth, who built the Labyrinth for King Minos. Imprisoned on Crete with his son [b]Icarus[/b], he made two pairs of wings from feathers and wax.

He warned Icarus to fly neither too low, where the sea spray would soak the feathers, nor too high. Icarus flew too close to the sun; the wax melted and he fell into the sea that now bears his name, the Icarian Sea.

talos.title: Talos
talos.text:
A giant man of [b]bronze[/b] - in most versions forged by the smith-god Ephestos - who guarded Crete for King Minos. He strode around the island [b]three times a day[/b], hurling boulders at approaching ships.

He had a single vein running from his neck to his ankle, sealed by a [b]bronze nail[/b]. In the story of the Argonauts, the sorceress [b]Medea[/b] brought about his death and the ichor - the divine blood - poured out. Talos is often called the first robot in literature.

thera.title: The Thera Eruption
thera.text:
Around [b]1600 BCE[/b] the volcano on the island of [b]Thera (Santorini)[/b], about 110 km north of Crete, erupted in one of the largest volcanic events in human history. It buried the Minoan town of [b]Akrotiri[/b] in ash - preserving its houses and beautiful frescoes, like a Bronze Age Pompeii.

Ash and tsunamis may have damaged Crete and its fleets. Some have suggested the eruption inspired Plato's later legend of Atlantis, though that remains speculation.

mycenaeans.title: The Mycenaeans
mycenaeans.text:
The Greek-speaking civilisation of the mainland, named after [b]Mycenae[/b] with its famous Lion Gate. Around [b]1450 BCE[/b] Mycenaeans took control of Knossos, and Linear B tablets in Greek replaced Linear A.

Theirs is the world remembered in Homer's [i]Iliad[/i] and [i]Odyssey[/i] - Agamemnon, Achilles, Odysseus. Their palaces fell in the Late Bronze Age collapse around 1200-1100 BCE, followed by the 'Greek Dark Ages' before the rise of classical Greece.

athens_contest.title: Athena and Poseidon
athens_contest.text: Two gods wanted Attica. [b]Poseidon[/b] struck the rock of the Akropolis with his trident and a spring of salt water leapt out; [b]Athena[/b] planted the first olive tree. The people judged the olive the better gift - food, oil and light - and the city became [b]Athens[/b]. Poseidon, angry, flooded the plain. Her sacred olive grew on the Akropolis ever after; when the Persians burned it, men said it put out a new shoot the very next day.

athens_salamis.title: The Wooden Walls
athens_salamis.text: When the Persians came, the oracle at Delphi told the Athenians to trust in their [b]wooden walls[/b]. [b]Themistokles[/b] said the walls were ships. He drew the Persian fleet into the narrow strait of [b]Salamis[/b] (480 BC), where its numbers were useless, and won. A runner's famous run from [b]Marathon[/b] to Athens, ten years before, is told by later writers: he gave the news of victory and died.

sparta_oracle.title: Love of Money
sparta_oracle.text: The Spartans said the Delphic oracle had warned them: '[b]Love of money, and nothing else, will destroy Sparta[/b].' Their lawgiver [b]Lykourgos[/b] had made their coins of iron, too heavy to hoard. Yet more than one Spartan king, among them [b]Leotychidas[/b], was exiled for taking bribes.

sparta_thermopylae.title: Thermopylai
sparta_thermopylae.text: In 480 BC King [b]Leonidas[/b] and three hundred Spartans, with their allies, held the narrow pass of [b]Thermopylai[/b] against the Persian army for three days, until a traitor showed the Persians a path round it. Told the Persian arrows would hide the sun, the Spartan [b]Dienekes[/b] answered: 'Good - then we shall fight in the shade.'

sparta_dioscuri.title: The Twin Stars
sparta_dioscuri.text: [b]Kastor[/b] and [b]Polydeukes[/b], the Dioskouroi, twin sons of Zeus and Leda, were Sparta's own heroes. Sailors saw them in the lights that burn on masts in a storm, and prayed to them for rescue. When Kastor died, Polydeukes shared his immortality with him: they live one day among the gods and one below, turn and turn about.

mycenae_walls.title: Cyclopean Walls
mycenae_walls.text: The walls of [b]Mykenai[/b] and [b]Tiryns[/b] are built of stones so huge that later Greeks said only the [b]Cyclopes[/b] - one-eyed giants, smiths of Zeus's thunderbolts - could have lifted them. Mykenai's gate is crowned by two stone lions. In the shaft graves inside, [b]Schliemann[/b] found gold death-masks (1876) and wired home that he had 'gazed on the face of Agamemnon'.

mycenae_atreus.title: The House of Atreus
mycenae_atreus.text: [b]Atreus[/b], king of Mykenai, killed his brother's sons and served them to him at a feast; a curse fell on his house. His son [b]Agamemnon[/b] led the Greeks to Troy, but at [b]Aulis[/b] Artemis held back the winds until he offered his daughter [b]Iphigeneia[/b]; in some tellings the goddess put a hind in her place. Agamemnon came home to be murdered by his wife - and so the curse ran on.

mycenae_heroes.title: Heroes of the Argolid
mycenae_heroes.text: [b]Perseus[/b], said to have founded Mykenai, killed the Gorgon and the sea-monster [b]Cetus[/b] to save [b]Andromeda[/b]. [b]Herakles[/b], born to the royal house, served the king of Mykenai for twelve labours; the second was the [b]Hydra[/b] of Lerna, whose heads grew back two for one until his nephew burned the stumps.

ionia_arche.title: The First Principle
ionia_arche.text: In the Ionian cities of the 6th century BC, thinkers began to explain the world without myths. [b]Thales[/b] of Miletos said everything is made of water - and was said to have foretold the solar eclipse of 585 BC. [b]Anaximenes[/b] said air; [b]Herakleitos[/b] of Ephesos said fire, and that everything flows; [b]Pythagoras[/b] of Samos said all things are number.

ionia_herostratos.title: Herostratos
ionia_herostratos.text: In 356 BC a man set fire to the great [b]temple of Artemis at Ephesos[/b], one of the Seven Wonders, so that his name would live for ever. The Ephesians executed him and forbade anyone to speak or write his name. The historian Theopompos wrote it down anyway: [b]Herostratos[/b].

cyclades_delos.title: Delos
cyclades_delos.text: Delos, the small island at the centre of the Cyclades ('the circling isles'), was said to have floated free until [b]Leto[/b], pursued by Hera's jealousy, gave birth there to [b]Apollo[/b] and [b]Artemis[/b]; then it was fixed to the sea-bed on four pillars. It became one of the holiest places in Greece: no one was allowed to be born or to die on it.

cyclades_isles.title: Gold, Obsidian and Marble
cyclades_isles.text: [b]Siphnos[/b] grew rich on gold and silver and sent Apollo a golden egg each year, until (the story goes) it cheated him with gilded lead and the sea flooded its mines. [b]Melos[/b] traded obsidian for thousands of years before metal. [b]Paros[/b] gave the finest white marble. On [b]Keros[/b], archaeologists found thousands of marble figurines, broken on purpose and laid together - no one knows why.
